lawyer:
Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md Ibrahim Khalil, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Abu Lokman ----- Petitioner
Vs
Commissioner of Customs & others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Awlad Ali J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Notification dated 17-6-1996 vide Annexure-F should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and as being unconstitutional and why the respondents should not be directed to levy and collect customs duty, VAT and other taxes in respect of the goods imported under L/C No. 1761296122 dated 30-10-96 on the basis of the invoice value. 

 2. The facts, in short, are that the petitioner is the proprietor of IM Corporation and carrying on business of import, inter alia, of Steel GI Pipe. The petitioner opened a Letter of Credit bearing No. 1761296122 dated 30-10-96 for an amount of US$ 37,267.90 for import of 8680 pieces of Steel GI Pipe under HS Code No. 7306.5000. The imported goods arrived at Chittagong Port on 20-1-97 under Commercial Invoice dated 25-11-96. In order to release the said consignment the petitioner through his clearing Agent, submitted bill of entry being C 56958 dated 22-1-97 for assessment and payment of Customs duty, VAT and other charges. When the respondent No.1 directed by an order dated 25-1-97 to assess the imported goods on the basis of Tariff Value. It has been contended that the petitioner is liable to pay the duties and taxes on the basis of Invoice value of the goods and the respondents arbitrarily imposed the Tariff Value without any factual or objective basis. 

 3. No affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the respondents to controvert the statements made in the writ petition. 

 4. Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, the learned Advocate, firstly, contended that the Tariff Value was introduced by Notification dated 17-6-96 which was published in the Official Gazette on 17-8-96 for GI Pipe of different sizes and description. But the petitioner imported GI Pipe of other size and description which do not come under the said SRO. Therefore, tariff value imposed by the impugned Notification is without jurisdiction. Second contention is that the tariff value was imposed by the impugned Notification having no objective basis of that as the value does not reflect the fair price on the value of the goods in the international market. He has further argued that the respondents have not produced any material before this court on the basis of which the tariff value was determined and notification was issued pursuant to section 25(7) of the Customs Act 1969 without considering the prevailing international market price. As regard his first contention no specific ground has been taken in the writ petition stating that the GI Pipe, which the petitioner imported, does not come with the purview of the impugned notification because description given in the notification is completely different from the description of the pipes imported by the petitioner. It appears that in the declaration on the bill of entry submitted by the petitioner the description of the goods as given is simply GI Pipe of 1½". In the computerized bill of entry description of the goods appeared to be GI Pipe as given in the impugned notification which was published on 11-8-96. Therefore, the first contention raised by the learned Advocate fails. It appears that the petitioner opened L/C on 30-10-96 and after arrival of the consignment the bill of entry was presented on 22-1-97. The impugned Notification introducing tariff value came into being on 17-6-96, which was published, in the official Gazette on 11-8-96. 

 5. Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder contends that although the notification was issued imposing tariff value prior to the presentation of the bill of entry but in determining the tariff value the authority did not take into consideration the objective basis or fair value or price in the international market. No materials have been produced before this Court under affidavit in support of the fixation of the tariff value. This court can justify the validity of the imposition of tariff value considering the papers annexed to the supplementary affidavit showing the invoice value of the similar kind of GI Pipes of the contemporary period. The papers annexed to the supplementary affidavit are commercial invoices of the goods imported by other importers showing the invoice value. From those invoices we cannot decide the question as to how the duty was imposed and what was the basis of assessment because the bills of entry relating to those invoices have not been presented before us and, as such, that cannot be the basis for determination of the question whether tariff value was imposed by the impugned notification or the goods were assessed to duty as per invoice value. The contention that assessment was made without having the objective basis or without considering the fair price in the international market does not hold good. 

 6. Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder pointed out paragraphs 19-20 of the judgment in the case of Mustafa Kamal and another vs Commissioner of Customs and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 1. In paragraph 19 it has been stated that "when the Government or the Customs authority in its affidavit-in-opposition annexes rebuttal materials to show that the prevalent international market price of any particular item is approximate to the impugned tariff value, the question of onus fades into insignificance and the High Court Division is then free to decide on the basis of documents annexed by both sides as to on whose side the scale is heavier. If the writ petitioner's documents carry more weight his case will be accepted. If the Government's documents carry better weight its case will be accepted.", In the instant case the respondent has not filed any affidavit-in-opposition annexing any papers showing price of the goods in the international market (If the value determined by any committee. The petitioner although lately annexed some documents to the supplementary affidavit that cannot be relied upon for the reasons we have already stated above. The unamended section 25(1) of the Customs Act reads as follows: 

 "25(1) The value of any imported goods shall be taken to be the normal price, that is to say, the price which they would fetch, on the date referred to in section 30 on a sale in open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other," 

 7. Sub-section (1) of section 25 indicates the normal price which again signifies the price which they would fetch on a sale in open market between the buyer and seller. The invoice value is the value mentioned in the invoice sent by the seller to the buyer importer. The invoice may contain the price of the goods which may not be the normal price as envisaged in. sub-section (1) of section 25. Sub section (7) of section 25 is in the following terms: 

 "(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the Government may be notification in the official Gazette, fix for the purpose of levying customs-duties, tariff values for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad valorem; 

 8. The Government in compliance with sub- section (7) of section 25 issued Notification on 17-6-96 that was published in the official Gazette on 11-8-96. The condition as laid down in sub-section (7) of section 25 has been completely fulfilled and the provision of the sub-section has been complied with as the Government imposed the tariff value by Notification in the official Gazette. How the tariff value was determined by the authority that has not been disclosed in the notification itself. The petitioner also has not produced any materials showing the fair international market price obtained from authentic sources. In such a situation we cannot call upon the authority to produce the documents or materials on the basis of which notification introducing tariff was issued. The authority before framing the Rules on 29-5-97 used to impose tariff value by notification in the official Gazette under sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act. Before 29-5-97 there was no rules governing the fixation of tariff value. The authority had to determine the tariff value according to the need of the hour to prevent inflow of foreign goods and to protect the indigenous industrial enterprise/concern from extermination, which objects coalesced with the aim of raising government revenue. From a plain reading of sub-section (7) of section 25 it appears to us that the Government realises highest duty by imposing tariff value by issuing Notification in the official Gazette as it is evident from the proviso that any imported or exported goods the declared value of which is higher than its tariff value fixed under this sub-section 7 shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value, In the decision cited by Mr Ramzan Ali Sikder it has not been said explicitly that sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Customs Act is contrary to the other provisions of the Customs Act and contrary to any provision of the Constitution, Rules have been framed for determination of tarif value and committee is constituted for such purpose. If the committee do not follow the rules framed on 25-9-97 in that case the importer can question the tariff value on the plea that the rules have not been adhered to in determining tariff and before issuing notification under the said sub section. Therefore, we do not find any substance in this Rule.
